title: The PLC scan cycle and why timers and one-shots misbehave
summary: Use the cyclic scan as a teaching model, then check the actual controller’s task, I/O and instruction behavior.

blocks.title: Read, solve, write, repeat
blocks.body: A simple cyclic PLC model samples inputs, executes logic in order and updates outputs. It is useful for learning scan effects, but not universal: modern controllers can update I/O asynchronously and run multiple tasks. Start by naming the model, then check the actual controller and task configuration.

nodes.title: 1. Read inputs
nodes.detail: Every physical input is copied into the input image table. The table is now frozen for the rest of the scan.

nodes.title: 2. Solve logic
nodes.detail: Execute rungs in order; writes to internal tags can affect later rungs in the same task execution.

nodes.title: 3. Write outputs
nodes.detail: The output image table is copied to the physical outputs, all at once.

nodes.title: Housekeeping
nodes.detail: Communication and diagnostics also take time. Measure the configured task/scan behavior instead of assuming a typical value.

blocks.heading: What happens between samples?
blocks.body: In this teaching model, a changed input is not seen until the next sample. On a controller with asynchronous I/O, separate reads can see different values within one logic execution. Use the platform’s supported buffering methods when a consistent snapshot is required. Input filtering and module update intervals also affect what is observed.

blocks.heading: Why timers misbehave
blocks.body: Separate timer timebase resolution from the interval at which logic observes its result. A controller can track time more finely than the task period, while the program reacts only when it executes. Retentive/non-retentive behavior, false-rung handling and skipped execution depend on the instruction and platform. Skipping a routine is not necessarily the same as executing its rung false. Verify all four conditions in the manual and a controlled test.

blocks.heading: Why one-shots misbehave
blocks.body: An edge detector compares the current sample with remembered state. It needs a defined execution schedule and its own correctly managed storage. A pulse entirely between executions may be missed. Conditional execution, shared storage or initialization can change behavior, but stale history alone does not guarantee double-firing. Identify which observed transition produced each pulse.

blocks.heading: The output that ignores you
blocks.body: Within one sequential execution, a later write to the same tag can replace an earlier write. Other tasks, forces and asynchronous I/O can complicate the result. Cross-reference all writers and task order. One deliberate owner per output makes the logic easier to diagnose.

blocks.heading: A scan-order bug in three rungs
blocks.code:
Rung 1:  Motor_Start_button ----( Motor_Contactor )
Rung 2:  Motor_Contactor ------( Motor_Running_Light )
... 400 rungs later ...
Rung 403: Overload_OK --------- ( Motor_Contactor )

Press the button:
- Scan N:   button read ON, rung 1 sets image bit ON,
            rung 2 sees it ON (same scan - it reads the
            image table), light comes on.
- Scan N:   rung 403 also writes the same coil. Whatever
            Overload_OK says wins, because it is later.
The button appears to do nothing. It did - for 400 rungs.

blocks.heading: Symptom to scan-cycle cause
rows: Unexpected timer result after a skipped routine
Check the timer’s documented skipped-execution behavior
History, initialization or another writer differs from the assumption
Pulse may fall between observations or be removed by filtering
Review input filtering, module timing and appropriate capture hardware
Output does not follow the rung being watched
Another writer, force or task may intervene
Test initialization, disable and resume explicitly

blocks.heading: Check the model
blocks.prompt: In the simplified model, the input is sampled every 12 ms with no hardware capture or filtering. A 5 ms pulse arrives. What can the program see?
options: The pulse, reliably, because inputs are real-time
The pulse only if it happens to span an input-read phase
Nothing - pulses under the scan time are always lost
A stretched 12 ms version of the pulse
blocks.explanation: The pulse is observed only if one sample falls inside its high interval. It is not reliably captured and not necessarily a 50/50 chance. For uniformly random phase in this ideal model, 5/12 of arrivals overlap a sample. Real modules add filtering and update behavior.
blocks.correctFeedback: Right - it is a sampling problem, not a logic problem.
blocks.wrongFeedback: Think about when the input image table gets written: once per scan. The pulse exists only in the real world, and the program only reads the table.
